messages.author: ec905fb18019a40d
messages.subject: control the number of knots
parts:
Hi all,


I am starting to use INLA package. 


About my data, I am trying to know the spatial distribution of fDOM in the platform sea. I have 4 samplings (4 months), in each month 20 points (4 stations x 5 radials). In each station, I have a profile of fDOM so I have in each station the continuous covariate depth, fDOM, Temperature, Salinity, Turbidity and Oxygen.


after some reading I think that my mesh could be the attached one in the figure. the black points are the 20 sampling points. The same spatial structure has been followed during 4 months.


In GAMM models I use the parameter k to control the smooth, for example for the covariates Salinity and temperature the code in gam would be " s(Salinity,k=4) +s(Temperature,k=4)"  How can I reduce the number of knots in the continous covariates of a INLA model?


Should I include a new parameter in this part  " f(Temp, model="rw2") + f(Depth, model="rw2")+ f(Sal, model="rw2")+ f(Transmisivity, model="rw2")+ f(Oxygen, model="rw2")"  of the INLA model?


thanks in advance

Enrique


Here, you can see all the codes from the construction of the mesh to the model. If anyone need the matrix I don´t mind to attach it. 



### Mesh

args(inla.nonconvex.hull)

loc <- cbind(CTD$ScaledLong,CTD$ScaledLat)

coords <- as.matrix(CTD[,47:48]) 

bound4 <- inla.nonconvex.hull(coords, concave=0.1, resolution=c(50, 50))

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=bound4, cutoff=0.1, max.edge=c(.2,.5))

plot(mesh);points(loc, col = 1, pch = 16, cex = 1.5) ## un candidato 123


### SPDE, spatial index, matrix A


spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh, prior.range=c(0.1, 0.05), prior.sigma=c(1, 0.05))

spatial.indices <- inla.spde.make.index("spatial", n.spde=spde$n.spde)

loc.obs <- as.matrix(cbind(CTD$Long, CTD$Lat))

A.obs <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc.obs)


### 

stack.obs <- inla.stack(data=list(fdom=CTD$fdom),  

  A=c(A.obs, 1),

  effects=list(spatial.indices,

                     list(Intercept=1,Month=inla.group(CTD$MonthN), Radial=inla.group(CTD$Radial2), SeaDist=inla.group(CTD$StationN),Temp=inla.group(CTD$TempCTD),Depth=inla.group(CTD$DepthRound),Sal=inla.group(CTD$SalCTD),Transmisivity=inla.group(CTD$Transmisividad),Oxygen=inla.group(CTD$O2mglCTD))),tag="observed")    


### model including random spatial and 5 continous variables                   

model9 = fdom ~ -1 + Intercept + Month+  f(Temp, model="rw2") + f(Depth, model="rw2")+ f(Sal, model="rw2")+ f(Transmisivity, model="rw2")+ f(Oxygen, model="rw2") + f(spatial, model=spde)

result9 <- inla(model9, data=inla.stack.data(stack.obs, spde=spde),control.compute=list(dic=TRUE), 

                 family="gaussian",

  control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack.obs),compute=TRUE))

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] control the number of knots
parts:
In the common GAMM packages like mgcv, the smooth models are defined as spline functions with a fixed, usually small, number of knots.
In INLA, the smooth models are handled more as Gaussian processes on continuous domains.
That means for example, that even though the meshes have a fixed number of "knots", this should not be used to control the smoothness of the model, but rather chosen so that the discrete model is able to represent whatever smoothness the continuous model leads to, and the parameters of the model (like the smoothing penalty for spline models; for spatial models usually also the correlation range parameter) is what controls the smoothness;
in spde models the triangles should be small enough that you don't see any obvious triangle patterns in the results.

In essence, it's like taking the limit k --> infinity, and making sure that the smoothing penalty is properly defined.
If your estimates of a rw2 model are less smooth than you think is reasonable, you can consider the prior settings for the model; you would then need to understand how to encode your "I think this is reasonable" information into that.

For 1D models, there _is_ however a way of achieving a similar "limited number of knots" effect using an SPDE version of the rw2 model, whih supports second order B-splines with limited number of knots.  The "Tokyo rainfall" example in the "read this first" SPDE tutorial on r-inla.org can be modified to produce such a model.  However, it's not something I would recommend, as models with a number of knots so small that it actually has an effect on the estimates is arguably needlessly artificial; the knot count and placement is a subjective model choice. In contrast, the continuous Gaussian process approach is non-parametric alternative.

Finn
